title: No Farm. No License. No Quarantine: Why Vietnam's Dog Trade Defies All Safety Standards
excerpt: Vietnam's dog meat industry operates without verified quarantine records, licensed breeding facilities, or health inspections. The trade's core defense—that dogs are farm-raised—collapses under scrutiny of actual enforcement gaps and documented pet theft.
body_html:
Every defense of Vietnam's dog meat trade rests on a single claim: the animals come from farms, not stolen pets. Ask for proof—a license number, a quarantine certificate, a facility inspection—and the answer never comes. Because there are no farms. There is only an unregulated supply chain that trades in stolen family companions and uninspected animals, moving them through darkened alleys and unmonitored checkpoints while rabies and other zoonotic pathogens travel with every shipment.

The Farm Defense Collapses Under Light

Vietnam's Ministry of Agriculture has never published verified records of licensed dog breeding facilities operating under national animal welfare or quarantine standards. The industry's repeated claim—that commercial dog operations exist under legitimate agricultural oversight—has no public documentation. When journalists and animal welfare investigators request facility lists, inspection records, or quarantine certificates, silence is the only answer.

This is not bureaucratic oversight. This is the absence of any regulatory framework at all. A legitimate agricultural sector produces auditable records: breeding permits, veterinary health certificates, movement documentation. Vietnam's dog meat supply chain produces none of these. Instead, it produces stolen pets lifted from family homes and transported in unmarked vehicles across provincial boundaries, evading the very checkpoints that should enforce quarantine protocols.

The contrast is sharp: Thailand's government published explicit quarantine and slaughter regulations before any commercial operation could claim legitimacy. Vietnam has published no equivalent standard. The trade operates in a legal and epidemiological vacuum by design.

Stolen Pets, Not Livestock: The Supply Chain Reality

Court records across Vietnam document the mechanics of the trade: syndicates using poison baits and theft to capture companion animals, then moving them through overnight transport networks that bypass all quarantine checkpoints. A dog stolen from a Hanoi family on Monday reaches a slaughterhouse in a neighboring province by Tuesday—no health certificate, no quarantine observation, no pathogen screening.

This is not an exaggeration. It is the documented operational model. When police conduct seizures, they recover animals bearing collar marks, tags, and behavioral characteristics of long-term companions. They find evidence of poison bait campaigns in residential neighborhoods. They intercept transport vehicles carrying animals with no documentation whatsoever.

The farm defense cannot survive this reality. Legitimate livestock operations do not steal animals from family homes. They do not use cyanide bait in city streets. They do not move product through clandestine overnight routes designed to evade inspection.

Rabies Has No Respect for Legal Fiction

Vietnam's public health system continues to report rabies exposures among families who encounter stolen dogs being transported or held before slaughter. The virus does not distinguish between a stolen pet and a farm animal. Once a person is bitten or scratched by an infected dog—whether a family companion or a transit animal—the clock begins. Post-exposure prophylaxis (immediate wound washing with soap and water, followed by urgent vaccination and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin) must begin within hours. Once symptoms develop, rabies is virtually 100% fatal.

The trade's absence of quarantine records means no one can verify whether an animal has been screened for rabies before entering the supply chain. The absence of licensed facilities means no one can verify that handlers have been trained in disease recognition or bite prevention. The absence of movement documentation means no one can trace an animal's origin or exposure history.

This is not a hypothetical gap. This is a documented public health vulnerability that expands with every unmarked shipment that crosses a provincial boundary without inspection.

Modern Vietnam Is Moving Forward

Across Vietnamese communities, support for ending the dog meat trade is measurable and growing. Families are choosing not to participate. Cities are shifting away from the practice. The trade persists not because it reflects Vietnamese culture or majority preference, but because it remains profitable for criminal syndicates operating in the regulatory void.

Abolition is not an attack on Vietnam. It is a Vietnamese demand for modernization, community safety, and the protection of family pets. It is a call to close the legal gaps that allow criminals to operate with impunity.

Sign SDE's national petition calling for complete abolition by 2030. Add your name to a public demand for transparent, enforceable regulations that protect Vietnamese families, their pets, and public health. The trade has no verified farms, no valid quarantine records, and no defensible claim to legitimacy. Modern Vietnam can close these gaps. Help make it happen.
